name: aburaage
sourceNote: Thin deep-fried tofu sheets, from the Japanese standard composition tables for abura-age. USDA carries a record called 'tofu, fried' at 270 kcal with 20 g of fat, and it is a different product — thicker, less thoroughly fried, and with carbohydrate this has almost none of — so the Japanese figure is the right one here. Published values scatter from 190 to 386 kcal for much the same reason. Treat this as an upper bound: any recipe that blanches the sheets in boiling water first, as the kitsune udon here does, pours a measurable amount of that 34 g of fat down the sink. mu 25 g is one sheet.
keeping: A week in the fridge in its packet, and it freezes for three months — freezing is the normal way to keep it, and the sheets separate from frozen with no thawing needed. The fat is what goes off: an old sheet smells of stale oil, tastes bitter, and no amount of simmering in dashi hides it. Once simmered in seasoning it keeps four days in its liquid and is arguably better on the second day.

name: all-purpose flour
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168894; rho from King Arthur, 120 g per cup spooned and levelled. Folate is total folate; the DFE figure for enriched flour is 291 ug.

name: apple
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171688, raw with skin. mu 182 g, USDA medium apple; the recipe peels it, which takes off about 15 g.
keeping: Six weeks in the fridge, in a bag, away from everything else — apples give off ethylene and will ripen and then rot whatever they sit next to.

name: baby corn
sourceNote: Fresh baby corn. FoodData Central lists only the canned product, which is saltier and softer; these are the declared values for the fresh vegetable. mu 8 g per ear.
keeping: A week in the fridge in a bag. It is sold both fresh and in tins — the tinned kind keeps unopened for years and needs draining and a good rinse, and once opened it goes in a box of fresh water in the fridge for 3 days.

name: baking powder
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 175040 (double-acting); rho 192 g per cup

name: banana
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 173944, raw banana. mu = 118 g, one medium peeled banana (7-8 inches), which is the USDA reference portion.

name: bay leaves
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170917, dried bay leaf. mu 0.2 g for one leaf. They are removed before eating, so this contributes almost nothing whichever way it is counted.

name: bean sprouts
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169952, mung beans, mature seeds, sprouted, raw. Mung sprouts are the thin white ones sold in every supermarket. Soybean sprouts — kongnamul, with the yellow bean head still on — are a different and larger sprout, nuttier and firmer, and are what a Korean recipe means; they run a little higher in protein and fat. Nothing in a panel turns on the difference, and mung sprouts are the ones that are actually available.
keeping: Two days, and that is generous. Bean sprouts are the most perishable thing in this collection: they are wet, they are cut, and they were grown warm. Keep them submerged in cold water in a covered box in the fridge, change the water daily, and they will make three or four. Slimy, brown-tipped or smelling of ammonia means finished. They do not freeze in any useful form.

name: beef brisket
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy, beef brisket raw, lean and fat together. Bought on the bone the figures are for the meat you get off it, not the weight you paid for — reckon on a third of a bone-in piece being bone.

name: beef sirloin
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168608, beef top sirloin, raw, trimmed to 1/8 inch fat.
keeping: Three days in the fridge, unwrapped from plastic and loosely covered on a plate — plastic film traps moisture against the surface and it goes slimy. Freezes 6 months whole, and it slices far more neatly half-frozen.

name: beetroot
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169145, raw beetroot. gramsPerUnit 150 is one medium beet, trimmed and peeled. The sodium is unusually high for a vegetable and is the beet's own, not seasoning.

name: bell peppers
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170427, raw red pepper. mu 119 g for one. Green peppers carry about a third of the vitamin C.
keeping: Two weeks whole in the fridge. Cut peppers keep 3 days in a box, and they freeze well sliced, which is worth doing with the last of a bag: they go soft on thawing, so use them where they are cooked anyway.

name: bicarbonate of soda
sourceNote: Sodium bicarbonate: no energy, and 27.36 g sodium per 100 g by formula mass (Na 22.99 of NaHCO3 84.01). rho 0.92 g/ml as a loose powder.

name: bird's eye chillies
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170108, raw red hot chilli peppers. mu 2 g for one bird's eye chilli.
keeping: Two weeks in the fridge in a paper bag. Better: freeze the lot whole in a bag on the day you buy them. They slice perfectly from frozen, lose nothing but their crunch, and keep 6 months, which is the difference between a jar of chillies you use and a black bag you throw away.

name: black pepper
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170931, ground black pepper. rho 0.47 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 2.3 g.

name: black tea
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 173227, beverages, tea, black, brewed, prepared with tap water — the brewed drink, not the leaf, which is the same convention this library uses for espresso. A recipe therefore lists millilitres of tea and says in its method how much leaf made them. Nutritionally it is water; the row exists so that a recipe using 400 ml of it resolves rather than reading as a coverage gap. Brewing it four times as strong as this record assumes changes nothing that shows up in a panel, only the caffeine, which the panel does not carry.

name: black vinegar
sourceNote: Chinkiang black vinegar. FoodData Central has no record of it, and it is nothing like the balsamic and red wine vinegars it does hold, so these are the declared values from a typical bottle rather than a measurement. Energy and sodium vary noticeably between brands; the rest are unknown and left so. Removed from this library in August 2026 when no recipe used it, and restored when the dry tantanmen wanted it — the note about buyability rather than presence in memories.md is exactly this case. The figures are the ones it had before, unchanged. Tagged `gluten`: Chinkiang vinegar is brewed from glutinous rice with wheat bran.
keeping: Indefinitely in the cupboard, tightly capped. It is already an acid and there is nothing in it to spoil; what it loses over a year or two is aroma rather than safety. Sediment at the bottom of an aged bottle is normal and is worth not pouring in. Do not refrigerate — cold flattens it.

name: bone-in chicken thighs
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171076, raw chicken thigh meat and skin, multiplied by a 70% edible yield because a recipe states bone-in thighs by the weight you buy. The yield is the assumption in this row; it runs 65-75% by size. Weigh the meat and use a gram override if it matters.
keeping: Two days in the fridge, on the bottom shelf. Freeze 4 months. If you are only using the meat, freeze the bones separately in a bag and add to it — six sets make a stock.

name: broccoli
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170379, raw. mu 608 g for one large head, untrimmed; florets come to roughly two-thirds of that.
keeping: A week in the fridge, unwashed, in a loose bag. Yellowing florets are on the way out but taste fine cooked; a slimy stem base does not — cut it back to white.

name: brown sugar
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168833; rho from King Arthur, 213 g per cup packed

name: carrots
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170393, raw. mu 61 g, USDA medium carrot.
keeping: Three weeks in the fridge in a bag with the leafy tops cut off — the tops go on drawing water out of the root. Limp carrots come back after an hour in cold water, and are then fine for anything cooked.

name: caster sugar
sourceNote: The same sugar as `granulated sugar` and the same USDA row — sucrose is sucrose — ground finer. It is a separate entry because it is a separate thing to buy and because the grind decides whether a recipe works: a filling that must not be beaten needs sugar that dissolves without beating. rho 0.87 g/ml, against 0.825 for granulated, since the finer crystals pack closer.

name: celery
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169988, celery, raw. mu 40 g is one medium stick. The 80 mg of sodium per 100 g is unusually high for a vegetable and is worth knowing when a recipe uses a lot of it in a stock.
keeping: Two weeks in the fridge, and the trick is worth the trouble: cut the leafy tops off, wrap the head tightly in foil rather than plastic, and it stays crisp for a fortnight instead of going rubbery in five days. Limp celery is not finished — stand the cut sticks upright in a jug of cold water in the fridge for an hour and they come back. The leaves are the most flavoured part and belong in a stock rather than the bin.

name: chicken bouillon powder
sourceNote: Chinese chicken bouillon powder (鸡精), from a typical label rather than FoodData Central. It is mostly salt and MSG; the sodium figure is the only one that matters here and it dominates the dish's total.

name: chicken breast
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171477 (skinless, roasted)
keeping: Two days in the fridge, on the bottom shelf so nothing under it catches a drip. Freeze in single pieces rather than a block, 4 months.

name: chicken stock

madeUp.note: One Knorr-sized cube to 500 ml of boiling water, which is what this count assumes. An Oxo cube is smaller and its packet says 190 ml — using Oxo at this rate gives stock about a third of the strength intended. Stock from a cube also carries several times the sodium of the ready-made stock this row's figures describe. Cubes are whole things, so a recipe wanting 200 ml still counts as one cube; use half of it, or make the full 500 ml and keep the rest.

sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 174538, ready-to-serve chicken stock. rho 1.0 g/ml. Stock made from a cube runs several times this in sodium.
keeping: Four days in the fridge once the carton is open, or freeze it — 250 ml portions in a bag, laid flat, are the useful unit. Home-made stock keeps 3 days and freezes for 6 months.

name: chicken thigh
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171479 (skinless, roasted)
keeping: Two days in the fridge. Thighs freeze better than breast — 4 months, and they come back juicy where breast comes back stringy.

name: chilli flakes
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171329, ground red pepper (cayenne). rho 0.34 g/ml, from a level tablespoon of coarse flakes at 5 g.
keeping: A year in a sealed jar out of the light. They fade rather than spoil, and heat goes before colour does.

name: chilli oil
sourceNote: Crispy chilli oil of the Lao Gan Ma type, from a typical jar rather than FoodData Central. It is roughly two-thirds oil and one-third fried solids, so a spoonful is mostly fat and the sodium is real. Plain chilli oil with no solids is nearer 880 kcal and carries almost no sodium — a different row if you use it. Tagged `peanut` for the dietary filters. Lao Gan Ma's crisp chilli oil contains peanuts as visible pieces, which is a genuine surprise in a jar most people think of as chilli and oil. Chilli oils without them exist; the label is the authority.
keeping: Three months in the cupboard, six in the fridge, cap on. The oil goes rancid before the chilli does. If it was made at home with fresh aromatics — garlic, ginger, shallot — the fridge is not optional and a month is the limit.

name: chilli powder
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170919, the American blend — chilli with cumin, oregano and salt in it, which is where the sodium comes from. British chilli powder is pure ground chilli and carries almost none.

name: chinese cabbage
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169975, raw napa cabbage. mu 1000 g is one head; napa runs from about 680 g to 1.4 kg and a supermarket one is near the middle.
keeping: Three weeks whole in the fridge, which is far longer than it looks like it should. Cut it from the base up and press cling film onto the cut face; the exposed leaf browns in a day, the rest is untouched. Never wash it before storing.

name: choy sum
sourceNote: USDA has no record for choy sum, so these are the figures for its nearest indexed relative, pak choi — USDA SR Legacy 170390, cabbage, chinese (pak-choi), raw. The two are the same species, Brassica rapa, differing in which part has been bred large. Sold and cooked by weight, so no per-bunch figure; a supermarket bundle runs 250 to 350 g. Gai lan is a different species and coarser, and these are still the best numbers available for it.
keeping: Four days in the fridge, wrapped loosely in a damp cloth or newspaper inside an open bag — sealed in plastic it yellows from the inside out. Stand it upright if there is room, the way it grew. It goes limp before it goes bad: a softened bunch will still stir-fry, a bunch with yellow leaves or hollow woody stems will not. Blanched, squeezed dry and frozen it keeps three months, for soups only.

name: clams in the shell
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171975, raw clam meat, multiplied by a 25% meat yield because a recipe states clams by the weight you buy, which is mostly shell. The yield is the assumption in this row: it runs 20-30% by species and size, so read these figures to within about a fifth of themselves. Weigh the shelled meat and use a gram override if it matters.
keeping: Cook them the day you buy them. Until then: in the fridge in a bowl, covered with a damp cloth, never sealed in a bag and never sitting in water — they are alive and both suffocate them. Throw out any that will not close when tapped.

name: cocoa powder
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169593, unsweetened cocoa powder. rho 0.4 g/ml, from a tablespoon at 6 g. The iron and magnesium are per 100 g of something used two spoonfuls at a time. Drinking chocolate is mostly sugar and is a different thing entirely.

name: coconut milk
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170173, coconut milk, canned — the thick tinned kind pressed from grated flesh, not the thin cartoned drink sold beside the dairy milk, which is a tenth of the fat and is not a substitute. mu 400 g is one standard tin. Almost all of the fat is saturated, which is why a tin of this reads alarmingly next to double cream and tastes lighter than it. Not tagged as a nut. UK and EU allergen labelling treats coconut as a fruit; the US FDA classifies it as a tree nut. Anyone filtering on nuts because of a US label should know the two disagree.
keeping: Two years unopened in the cupboard. Once open, three days in the fridge and out of the tin. It separates into a thick cap and a watery layer both in the tin and in the fridge, which is not a fault — warm it gently and stir, or shake the tin hard before opening. Freezes for three months in an ice cube tray and comes back grainy, which disappears the moment it is stirred into anything hot.

name: cooked rice
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169756, cooked white rice. Roughly a third of the energy of raw rice by weight, because it is two-thirds water.
keeping: This one is a safety question rather than a quality one. Cool it within an hour — spread it out, do not leave the pot on the hob — then fridge for one day only, and reheat until it is steaming all the way through. Rice left warm grows Bacillus cereus, which makes a toxin that reheating does not destroy. Freezes for a month and reheats better from frozen than from the fridge.

name: coriander
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169997, fresh coriander leaves (cilantro). rho 0.26 g/ml chopped. mu 30 g is one British supermarket bunch, stalks included.
keeping: Ten days in the fridge treated like flowers: stems in a glass of water, a bag loosely over the top, water changed every other day. The leaves freeze badly and the stems freeze well — chop the stems, freeze them flat, and use them where the recipe cooks them.

name: cornflour
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169698, cornstarch. rho 0.54 g/ml, from a level tablespoon at 8 g. Called cornflour in Britain and cornstarch in the US; the same thing.

name: cucumber
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168409, cucumber with peel, raw. mu 300 g is one British supermarket cucumber; the short ridged Chinese kind and the Persian ones are 150 to 200 g each and are the better buy for a smashed salad, having thinner skin, fewer seeds and more crunch. It is 95% water, which is the fact every cucumber salad is built around — see the salting step in Smashed Cucumber Salad.
keeping: A week in the fridge, wrapped loosely, and it is one of the few vegetables that genuinely prefers the door to the salad drawer: below about 7 degrees it pits and goes translucent. Keep it away from apples, bananas and tomatoes, whose ethylene turns it yellow in days. A cucumber that has gone soft at one end is finished at that end only; cut it back to firm flesh. Cut faces dry and sour within a day, so wrap the stub.

name: dark soy sauce
sourceNote: From a Pearl River Bridge superior dark soy bottle: 20 kcal, 4 g carbohydrate and 1 g protein per 15 ml tablespoon, scaled to 100 ml. Dark soy is thicker and sweeter than light and is used by the spoon rather than the splash. The sodium is the weakest figure here — brands run 5000 to 7000 mg per 100 ml and few of them print it — so treat it as an estimate. Not interchangeable with `light soy sauce`, which is saltier and thinner. Tagged `gluten` for the same reason as light soy sauce: it is brewed with wheat.
keeping: As for light soy — safe in the cupboard, better in the fridge if the bottle lasts more than a few months. It thickens in the cold, which is not a problem for a teaspoon at a time.

name: dashi

madeUp.note: A dashi packet is about 8 g of kombu and katsuobushi in a bag. Drop it into the cold water, bring it to the boil, simmer 3 to 5 minutes, lift it out and squeeze it. Brands differ over how far one goes — 400 to 500 ml is the usual range, and this row takes the generous end, so a strong-tasting packet wants a little more water than the count says. A packet cannot be halved, so a recipe wanting less than one packet’s worth still counts as one and the dashi comes out stronger than the figures in this row — brew the full 500 ml and freeze the rest in an ice cube tray, which is what the keeping note is for. Instant granules are the other route: about 1 tsp to 200 ml, and far saltier than the brewed figures in this row.

sourceNote: Awase dashi — kombu and katsuobushi — as the brewed liquid, which is the convention this library already uses for black tea and espresso: a recipe lists millilitres and its method says what made them. USDA has no record. These are the middle of the published analyses, which run 9 kcal, 1.7 to 2 g protein and 25 to 41 mg of sodium per 100 ml; the spread is real, because how much kombu and how long it steeped is the whole variable. Instant dashi powder is far saltier — often ten times this — and a recipe using it should expect the sodium figure to be a serious underestimate. Tagged `fish` for the dietary filters, which is the one worth knowing: nothing about the words kitsune udon says the bowl is built on a fish stock. Kombu dashi, made from the seaweed alone, is the vegan version and is what a shojin kitchen uses.
keeping: Three days in the fridge in a covered jar, and it is genuinely better on the day it is made — the aroma is the point and it is the first thing to go. Freezes for a month in an ice cube tray, which is the sensible way to keep it, since most recipes want 200 ml rather than a litre. Spent kombu and katsuobushi make a second, weaker batch (niban dashi) good for simmering, and then go in the bin.

name: digestive biscuits
sourceNote: McVitie's own published figures for the Original digestive, August 2026: 483 kcal, 21 g fat of which 10 saturated, 64 g carbohydrate of which 15 sugars, 7 g protein, 3.7 g fibre and 1.3 g salt per 100 g. Sodium here is that salt figure divided by 2.5. Sainsbury's own-brand is close enough to stand in either direction. gramsPerUnit 13.5 is one biscuit, so a 150 g base is eleven of them.

name: dijon mustard
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168579. rho 1.05 g/ml. Wholegrain is close enough to use the same row.
keeping: A year in the fridge once opened. It does not spoil so much as fade: the heat in mustard is volatile and an old jar is mostly sourness.

name: dill
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169381, fresh dill weed. rho 0.2 g/ml, from a tablespoon of chopped fronds at 3 g. The iron and calcium look startling and are per 100 g of a herb nobody eats 100 g of.

name: doubanjiang
sourceNote: Pixian chilli bean paste, from jar labels. rho 1.1 g/ml, from a tablespoon at 17 g. Brands differ by more than any figure here suggests: an aged Pixian paste is drier, saltier and less sweet than a supermarket doubanjiang, and the sodium spread across the shelf is roughly 5000 to 7000 mg per 100 g. Tagged `gluten` for the dietary filters. Pixian doubanjiang is fermented with wheat flour as well as broad beans; a few brands are wheat-free and say so.
keeping: Fridge once opened, where it keeps a year. Level the surface after each use and pour a film of oil over it: what spoils a bean paste is the air on the top, not the age of the jar. Always a clean dry spoon.

name: dried oregano
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171328. rho 0.2 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 1 g.

name: dried rice noodles
sourceNote: Dry weight, USDA SR Legacy rice noodles. gramsPerUnit 100 is one portion dry, which triples in weight once soaked and boiled — every figure here is for the dry noodle, as the recipe weighs it. Sweet potato starch noodles, which this dish is also made with, are a different row: almost no protein and around 340 kcal.

name: dried shiitake mushrooms
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168436, mushrooms, shiitake, dried — weighed dry, as a recipe lists them. They take up about four times their weight in water, so 10 g dry is 40 g soaked. mu 4 g is one medium cap. The zinc figure is unusually high for a vegetable and is USDA's. Dried are not a worse substitute for fresh here but a different ingredient: drying concentrates the guanylate that makes them taste of anything at all, which is why a soaked dried shiitake beats a fresh one in a broth and loses to it in a stir-fry.
keeping: A year in a sealed jar in a dark cupboard, and they only get more concentrated. Buy them whole rather than sliced. Once soaked they are perishable like any mushroom: two days in the fridge. The soaking water is worth keeping for stocks and braises — strain the grit out through a cloth — though not for anything that is supposed to stay pale, which it will not.

name: dried shrimp
sourceNote: Xia mi — small salted dried shrimp. USDA has no record and the published figures disagree: energy runs 198 to 253 kcal and protein 43 to 62 g per 100 g, depending mostly on how dry and how salted the batch is. This row takes 253 kcal with 58 g of protein and 2.5 g of fat, which is the top of that range and is at least self-consistent through the Atwater factors. Sodium is the figure to hold loosely: 2500 mg is a middle value in a range that runs past 4800, because salt is the preservative and brands differ enormously. A tablespoon is about 8 g, so even the low end puts 200 mg into a dish. Soak them and the soaking water carries a good deal of that salt away with it.
keeping: Six months in a sealed jar in the fridge rather than the cupboard, which is where they keep their colour and their smell — at room temperature they go from pink to grey-brown and develop a hard, fishy edge. A year in the freezer, and they can be used straight from it. They should smell of the sea and faintly sweet; a sharp ammoniac smell means they are past it.

name: dried squid
sourceNote: You you gan, from the Chinese food composition table. These are the figures for the dry squid as weighed, which is how a recipe measures it — it takes up about three times its weight in water on soaking, so a soaked figure would be a third of these. The cholesterol is genuinely that high; squid is one of the densest sources of it in any kitchen.

name: dried thyme
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170938. rho 0.2 g/ml. The iron figure is real and is an artefact of grinding: dried thyme picks up iron from the mill.

name: dried wheat noodles
sourceNote: Plain Chinese dried wheat noodles (gua mian) — flour, water and salt, no egg — weighed dry as a recipe lists them. FoodData Central has no record of them; its Chinese noodle entries are all fried chow mein, which is a different food. These are the middle of the published brand labels, which cluster at 355 to 375 kcal and 11 to 13 g of protein. The figure worth knowing is the sodium: salt goes into the dough, so a dry Chinese noodle carries several hundred milligrams per 100 g where dry Italian pasta carries six, and most of that stays in the noodle rather than leaving in the water. 400 mg is a middling label and brands run from 300 to well over 1000, so check the packet if it matters. A different row from `egg noodles`, which are yellow, springy and Cantonese, and from `spaghetti`, which is durum and holds its bite differently. mu 100 g is one portion. They roughly double in weight boiled.
keeping: A year in the packet in a dry cupboard, and the packet is worth closing properly with a clip — dried noodles take up damp and then dry out warped and brittle. Cooked and drained they keep two days in the fridge tossed with a little oil so they do not weld into a block, and they come back in 20 seconds of boiling water.

name: dried wood ear mushrooms
sourceNote: Black fungus, weighed dry. Published figures scatter badly and some are plainly wrong — several product labels give 343 to 357 kcal with zero protein, which cannot be true of a food every laboratory measurement puts at about 12% protein. These are the Chinese food composition table's figures for dried wood ear, which agree closely with a published laboratory analysis at 208 kcal and 14.1 g of protein. The iron figure of 97 mg per 100 g is startling and is what the tables say; a 10 g portion is a gram of dried fungus's worth of it and the absorption is another question. It swells five or six times, so 10 g dry is a generous bowl.
keeping: Two years in a sealed bag in a dark cupboard; dried fungus is close to indestructible. Once soaked it is perishable and must be treated like any mushroom: cook it the same day, and never leave rehydrated wood ear standing at room temperature for hours, which is the one genuine food-safety warning attached to this ingredient. Soaked and cooked, it keeps three days in the fridge and its texture survives completely.

name: dry white wine
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 174837, table white wine. rho 0.99 g/ml. Most of the energy is alcohol, and most of the alcohol boils off in a sauce reduced hard, so treat the kcal as an upper bound rather than a figure.
keeping: Three days in the fridge with the cap on once opened, and a week if you pour it into a smaller bottle so there is less air on top. Past that it is vinegar in slow motion — still usable in a braise, no longer usable in a sauce.

name: duck breast
sourceNote: Raw duck breast with the skin on, from supermarket labels rather than FoodData Central, because USDA's two nearest records bracket it uselessly: 'meat only' is 135 kcal and 'meat and skin' for a whole duck is 404, and a breast sits between them since its skin covers proportionally less meat than a whole bird's does. Read the figure as an upper bound — the fat is almost all in the skin and the cap, and rendering it out over low heat, which is the only sensible way to cook a duck breast, leaves a good deal of it in the pan. mu 180 g is one supermarket breast.
keeping: Three days in the fridge on a plate, and better uncovered on the bottom shelf if there is room — a dry skin is the whole game with duck and a day uncovered scores it far better than any amount of patting. Three months frozen; defrost in the fridge overnight. Rendered duck fat is the by-product worth keeping: strain it into a jar and it lasts six months in the fridge and roasts the best potatoes you will make.

name: egg
sourceNote: USDA Foundation 748967 (whole, raw); mu 50 g, USDA large egg without shell
keeping: Three weeks in the fridge, pointed end down so the yolk stays centred. To test one, put it in a bowl of water: it lies flat when fresh, stands on end at about three weeks, and floats when it should be thrown away. Whites freeze perfectly, yolks do not.

name: egg noodles
sourceNote: USDA record for noodles, egg, dry, enriched — weighed dry, as a recipe lists them. They roughly double in weight boiled. This covers both the medium egg noodles every UK supermarket sells and the thin wonton noodles from an Asian supermarket, which differ in thickness rather than in composition; the thin ones cook in 90 seconds and the medium in four minutes. Enriched noodles carry added iron and folate, which is why those two columns look high for a plain wheat product.
keeping: Two years in the packet in a dry cupboard. Fresh egg noodles from the chiller are a different thing entirely: five days in the fridge, three months frozen, and they go into boiling water straight from the freezer. Cooked noodles keep two days in the fridge tossed with a teaspoon of oil to stop them welding, and never in soup.

name: egg tofu
sourceNote: Japanese standard composition tables for tamago-dofu: 79 kcal, 6.5 g protein and 5.3 g fat per 100 g. USDA has no record. Two related products share the name and this row is a compromise between them — Japanese tamago-dofu is egg set with dashi and eaten cold, while the yellow tube sold as egg tofu or Japanese tofu in Chinese supermarkets is soy milk and egg together, usually with a little starch, so it runs slightly lower in protein and higher in carbohydrate. The tube is what the recipes here use and its own label is the better guide. Sodium is the least certain figure: it is seasoned in the making, published values scatter widely by brand, and 390 mg is the middle of them. mu 250 g is one standard tube, though they run from 150 g to 300 g.
keeping: Unopened, up to the date on the tube — a month or so — in the fridge, and it must stay cold. Once opened it is two days, submerged in cold water in a covered box with the water changed daily, exactly as for silken tofu. It does not freeze: the egg and soy protein separate and it thaws into a spongy, weeping thing with none of the texture that was the point. Buy the tube intact; one that has gone soft or is swollen at the ends has fermented and goes in the bin.

name: egg white
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 172184, raw egg white. gramsPerUnit 33 is the white of one large egg. The counterpart to the `egg yolk` row and just as necessary: the white is where nearly all an egg's sodium is and none of its fat or cholesterol, so a recipe that separates them cannot be counted in whole eggs.

name: egg yolk
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 172183, raw fresh egg yolk. gramsPerUnit 17 is the yolk of one large egg. A separate row from `egg` because they are not interchangeable in a panel: gram for gram the yolk carries six times the fat of a whole egg and nearly all of its cholesterol, so a recipe using three yolks and one whole egg counted as four eggs would understate both by a wide margin.

name: espresso
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171891, beverages, coffee, brewed, espresso, restaurant-prepared, unsweetened. rho 1.0 g/ml. Nutritionally it is water with a little magnesium and potassium in it — 80 mg of magnesium per 100 g, which is the one figure worth knowing — and the row exists so that a recipe using 300 ml of it resolves rather than reading as a coverage gap. This row cited 171890 until August 2026, which is drip coffee at 2 kcal rather than espresso at 9; the id was wrong and the numbers were right.

name: evaporated milk
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170878, milk, canned, evaporated — unsweetened. Sweetened condensed milk is a different tin with four times the sugar and is not a substitute. rho 1.07 g/ml, denser than milk because that is what it is: whole milk with about 60% of its water boiled off, so every figure here runs about 2.2 times the corresponding one for milk.
keeping: Unopened, two years in the cupboard. Once the tin is open, four days in the fridge and not in the tin — decant it into a jar, because the exposed metal taints it. It freezes for three months in a tub and comes back slightly grainy, which does not matter in a batter.

name: fatty pork mince
sourceNote: Interpolated between USDA SR Legacy 168318 (96% lean) and 168333 (84% lean) to give 10% fat, which is what a stir-fry wants — 5% mince gives up no fat to fry the aromatics in. A 20% mince runs nearer 250 kcal.
keeping: Two days in the coldest part of the fridge, in the bottom of the packet on a plate in case it leaks. Mince spoils faster than a whole cut because grinding puts the surface everywhere. Freeze it flat in a bag on the day you buy it — 3 months, and it defrosts in an hour rather than overnight.

name: fermented black beans
sourceNote: Douchi, the dry salted black soybean sold in bags and tubs. Figures are a soybean base adjusted for the salt it is cured in; no USDA entry exists for it. The sodium is the load-bearing number and it is high enough that rinsing before use is standard — this row is for unrinsed beans, so treat it as a ceiling. rho 0.8 g/ml, from a tablespoon at 12 g.
keeping: A year in a sealed jar in the cupboard, and longer in the fridge. They are salted and dry, so what ruins them is damp — a wet spoon or a bag left open makes them clump and mould.

name: filter coffee
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171890, beverages, coffee, brewed, prepared with tap water. Drip or filter coffee, and a quarter the strength of the espresso row next to it — they are separate records for good reason and are not interchangeable by volume.

name: firm tofu
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 172475, tofu raw firm prepared with calcium sulfate. The calcium is the coagulant, not the bean: a nigari-set block runs nearer 130 mg per 100 g, so treat 683 as specific to calcium-sulfate tofu and read the packet. gramsPerUnit 400 is a supermarket block. Figures were read off aggregators of that entry rather than FoodData Central itself, which could not be reached from the machine this row was written on; they cross-check against its 126 g serving (iron 3.35 mg, potassium 299 mg, sodium 18 mg).
keeping: Once the packet is open: submerged in fresh cold water in a box, in the fridge, water changed every day, 4 days. Out of water it dries and sours in two. It also freezes — it comes back spongy and full of holes, which is a fault in this recipe and a virtue in a braise.

name: fish sauce
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 174288. rho 1.2 g/ml. The sodium is not a misprint and it dominates any dish using it.
keeping: The cupboard is fine and it keeps a year, though it darkens. The white crystals that appear at the bottom or round the cap are salt, not spoilage.

name: five-spice powder
sourceNote: Star anise, cassia, clove, fennel and Sichuan pepper, ground. No USDA entry exists for the blend, so these are the figures of comparable ground whole spices and every one is an estimate. A teaspoon weighs about 2 g, so its contribution to any panel is smaller than the rounding — the row is here so that a recipe using it resolves. rho 0.4 g/ml.

name: flat-leaf parsley
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170416, fresh. rho 0.26 g/ml, from a level tablespoon of finely chopped leaves at 3.8 g. mu 30 g is one British supermarket bunch, stalks included.
keeping: Two weeks, stems in water in the fridge with a bag over the top. Sturdier than coriander and can also be washed, dried and frozen chopped, where it keeps its flavour if not its shape.

name: fried shallots
sourceNote: Crisp fried shallots from a tub, from a typical label rather than FoodData Central. They are shallots deep-fried until dry, so most of the weight is the frying oil — which is why the energy is nearer an oil's than an onion's. rho 0.2 g/ml.
keeping: A month in an airtight jar, and they must be properly cold before the lid goes on or the steam softens them. They are fried, so they eventually go rancid rather than stale.

name: garlic
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169230 (raw); mu 3 g, USDA one clove
keeping: Whole heads keep two months somewhere dark, dry and airy — not the fridge, where they sprout and go rubbery, and not a sealed jar. Peeled cloves keep a week in the fridge in a closed box. A green shoot inside a clove is bitter: split the clove and flick it out.

name: garlic powder
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171325. rho 0.65 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 3.1 g. Garlic granules are the same thing more coarsely ground.

name: gelatine
sourceNote: USDA figures for gelatins, dry powder, unsweetened: 85.6 g of protein and essentially nothing else, which is what makes the energy figure misleading — 10 g of it sets a litre and contributes 34 kcal to four servings. mu 1.7 g is one leaf, so five leaves are 8.5 g and a British sachet is about 12 g. The id is left off rather than guessed, since USDA carries several gelatin records and the sweetened dessert-powder ones are a different food entirely. Leaves and powder are interchangeable by weight; leaves are easier to measure and dissolve more reliably. Tagged `meat` and `pork` for the dietary filters: gelatine is boiled from hide and bone, and the leaf gelatine sold in British supermarkets is porcine unless it says otherwise. Beef and fish gelatines exist and agar is the vegetarian substitute, which sets firmer and does not melt in the mouth the same way.

name: ginger
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169231, raw root ginger. rho 0.41 g/ml, from a level tablespoon of minced ginger at 6 g.
keeping: Three weeks in the fridge unpeeled, in a paper bag rather than plastic, which sweats and makes it mouldy. Better: freeze the whole root and grate it from frozen straight into the pan — it grates finer frozen than fresh and never needs peeling.

name: glass noodles
sourceNote: USDA record for noodles, chinese, cellophane or long rice (mung beans), dehydrated — weighed dry, as a recipe lists them. They take up about three times their weight in water. Despite being made from mung beans they carry almost no protein: the process extracts pure starch and washes everything else away, which is why the protein column reads 0.16 g and is not a typo. Nutritionally this is starch, and the reason to use it is texture.
keeping: Two years in the packet in a dry cupboard; there is nothing in them to spoil. Once soaked they are perishable and clump into a solid mass within a few hours, so soak only what a dish needs and cut the bundle with scissors before soaking, or you will be fighting a metre-long tangle in the bowl.

name: gochugaru
sourceNote: Korean coarse chilli flakes, from brand labels rather than FoodData Central, which has no record for them: about 320 kcal, 12 g of protein and very little sodium per 100 g. Only the macros and the two figures worth knowing are recorded; the rest are left blank rather than borrowed from a different chilli, because it is used a spoon at a time and nothing turns on them. It is not interchangeable with the chilli powder or the sichuan chilli powder already in this library — gochugaru is coarse, bright red, sweet and only mildly hot, and substituting a fine hot powder turns a Korean salad into something painful and dull at once. rho 0.42 g/ml.
keeping: Six months in the freezer, which is where Korean kitchens keep it and where it holds its colour; a year in a sealed jar in a dark cupboard at the cost of fading from red to brown, and the colour is half of what it is for. Buy the coarse flakes rather than the powder unless a recipe asks otherwise.

name: golden syrup
sourceNote: Lyle's own published figures: 317 kcal, 79 g carbohydrate of which 79 g sugars, 0.3 g protein, no fat, and 0.27 g in the salt row per 100 g. Sodium here is that salt figure divided by 2.5, which gives 108 mg — several aggregators reprint the 0.27 g straight into a sodium column, which is two and a half times too much. Inverted cane syrup, so it is glucose and fructose rather than sucrose, which is why it does not crystallise. rho 1.43 g/ml.
keeping: Indefinitely in the cupboard with the lid on, and it does not need the fridge — the sugar concentration is its own preservative. Wipe the rim before closing it or the lid welds itself shut. If it has gone cloudy or grainy it has crystallised rather than spoiled: stand the tin in hot water for ten minutes and it clears.

name: granulated sugar
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169655; rho from King Arthur, 198 g per cup

name: grapefruit
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 174670, grapefruit, raw, pink and red. mu 230 g is the segments off one fruit, membranes discarded. It stands in for pomelo, which is what a mango pomelo sago is supposed to have and which no ordinary supermarket carries — pomelo is milder and drier and its strands hold up better, and pink grapefruit is the substitution every home version makes. Grapefruit interacts with a long list of prescription drugs and pomelo does the same; if that applies to you, leave it out and the dessert still works.
keeping: A week on the counter, three in the fridge, and it is one of the few fruits genuinely better cold. Segments broken into strands go limp within hours, so do that last of all, at the table if you can.

name: greek yogurt
sourceNote: USDA 330137 (plain, nonfat); rho 1.04 g/ml
keeping: A week after opening. Pour off the whey that gathers on top rather than stirring it in if you want it thick, and keep the spoon that goes in clean — yogurt spoils from what is put into it.

name: ground cardamom
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170923. rho 0.41 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 2 g. USDA reports no sugar or folate figure for cardamom, so both are left unknown.

name: ground cinnamon
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171320. rho 0.53 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 2.6 g.

name: ground cumin
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170924. rho 0.45 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 2.1 g.

name: ground sichuan pepper
sourceNote: Hua jiao mian: the husk of the Sichuan peppercorn, ground. There is no USDA entry and no reliable table for it, so these are the figures of a comparable dried whole spice and every one of them is an estimate. It contributes about a gram per serving to any dish that uses it, so the error it can introduce to a panel is smaller than the rounding — it is here so that a recipe using it resolves, not because the numbers are worth much. rho 0.4 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 2 g.
keeping: Three months, and this is the shortest life of any spice here. It is entirely aroma, and ground it is gone within a season — buy the whole husks, keep them a year in a jar, and grind what a dish needs. If yours has been open two years it is doing nothing at all.

name: guanciale
sourceNote: Cured pork jowl. No USDA entry exists for it. Checked in August 2026 against Italian product labels, which give 655 to 691 kcal and about 71 g of fat per 100 g — this row's 655 and 69 are the bottom of that range, so if anything it understates. Protein is the figure that moves most between producers, from 6.5 g to 12 g depending on how long it was hung. Beware the English-language nutrition aggregators here: several report guanciale at around 400 kcal and 30 g fat, which is pancetta's composition, not jowl's. Pancetta is the substitute, and it is leaner.

name: hot pot base paste
sourceNote: Spicy Sichuan hot pot base, the solid block sold for making hot pot broth, from packet labels. It is mostly beef tallow and chilli, which is why it is half fat and a fifth of that saturated. rho 1.0 g/ml is nominal: it is a solid at room temperature and a spoon of it is packed rather than poured. Tagged `meat` for the dietary filters: a Chongqing base is built on beef tallow, which is why it sets solid. Vegetarian bases are sold alongside and are usually labelled so in English.
keeping: Fridge once opened, 3 months, or freeze the block in portions the size you use — it is mostly beef tallow, so it cuts cleanly from frozen. Rancid fat is what fails first here, and it smells of old crayons.

name: icing sugar
sourceNote: Confectioners' sugar: granulated sugar milled fine with about 3% cornflour as an anti-caking agent. FoodData Central carries a record for powdered sugar which could not be reached from this machine, so these are `granulated sugar`'s figures with that cornflour fraction folded in — 389 kcal against 387, and 97 g of sucrose against 99.8 g of total carbohydrate. The difference is a rounding error in any recipe and the reason for a separate row is not the numbers, it is that icing sugar and caster sugar are not interchangeable in a shortcrust: icing sugar dissolves into the butter without creaming and gives the sandy, melting crumb a cookie crust is made of, and caster sugar in the same dough gives a biscuit that snaps. rho 0.51 g/ml sifted, from a cup at 120 g.
keeping: Indefinitely in a sealed container in a dry cupboard. It has no water in it and nothing can grow on it; what ends a bag is damp, which turns it to lumps that no sieve recovers. If it has set solid the bag was not closed. Sift it before use whatever its condition — even a fresh bag has lumps, and a lump of icing sugar in a tart crust bakes as a hole.

name: japanese curry roux
sourceNote: A block of S&B Golden Curry, from the box: 462 kcal, 28 g of fat of which 17 saturated, and 45 g of carbohydrate per 100 g. Sodium is worked out from the per-serving figures rather than the per-100 g salt line, and deliberately so — the label's per-serving numbers for energy, fat and carbohydrate all scale cleanly to its per-100 g ones, and its 2.2 g of salt per 18.4 g block scales to about 12 g per 100 g, while a '1.882 g per 100 g' figure that circulates online reconciles with nothing. Twelve grams of salt is 4760 mg of sodium, which makes this the second saltiest thing in this library after soy sauce. It is used 20 g at a time, so a portion carries about 950 mg. Brands and heat levels differ; the box is the authority, not this row. mu 20 g is one block, though they run 18 to 25 g. Tagged `gluten`, `soy` and `dairy` for the dietary filters. The box is the authority and this is the common case: the roux is a wheat-flour roux, most brands declare soy, and many declare milk. Vegetarian and allergen-free roux blocks are sold and are labelled clearly.
keeping: A year in the box in a dry cupboard, and the foil tray inside keeps unused blocks fine once it is opened — fold the flap down and put the box back. The fat can bloom to a pale surface film in a warm kitchen, which looks wrong and is harmless. Do not refrigerate: the block sweats and then crumbles.

name: jasmine rice
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168878, raw long-grain white rice; jasmine is the same composition. rho 0.8 g/ml, from a 200 g cup.

name: lap cheung
sourceNote: Cantonese cured sausage, from the Chinese food composition table's entry for guang shi xiang chang and checked against packet labels. gramsPerUnit 50 is one link. The sugar is not an error: lap cheung is cured with a great deal of it, which is why it caramelises where it touches the pan and why a recipe using it wants less sugar elsewhere. Tagged `soy` as well as `meat` and `pork`: nearly every brand is cured with soy sauce, and most with rose wine too, so anyone avoiding alcohol should read the packet.

name: lean pork
sourceNote: USDA figures for pork, fresh, loin, whole, separable lean only, raw — the cut sold as lean pork and what a Cantonese recipe means by shou rou. Vitamin D is left blank on purpose: the figure the sources returned was 22 ug per 100 g, roughly forty times what any pork contains and plainly a unit error, and a blank is better than a wrong number. Pork shoulder trimmed of its fat is a little fattier than this and behaves the same way.
keeping: Three days in the fridge on a plate on the bottom shelf, loosely covered so the surface dries rather than sweats. Six months frozen, and better sliced first and frozen flat in a bag — it defrosts in twenty minutes that way and takes a marinade straight after. Slicing thinly is easiest when the meat is half frozen, which is worth arranging on purpose. Defrost in the fridge, never on the counter.

name: leek
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169246, leeks, bulb and lower leaf-portion, raw — the white and pale green, which is the part a recipe uses. mu 90 g is one trimmed leek. It stands in here for naganegi, the Japanese long onion, which is what a Japanese recipe translated as 'leek' actually means: milder, more tender, and closer to an oversized spring onion than to a European leek. No table carries naganegi separately and the two are close enough that nothing in a panel turns on it.
keeping: Two weeks in the fridge, unwashed, wrapped loosely — and wrapped, because a leek will scent butter and cheese through a fridge shelf. The outer layer goes slimy first and peels off, leaving the rest fine. Grit hides between the layers well below where it looks clean: split the leek lengthways and fan it under a running tap rather than rinsing the outside. Sliced, it freezes for three months and goes into a pan from frozen, though it will never be crisp again.

name: lemon
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 167746, flesh without peel. mu 84 g, USDA's medium lemon. A lemon cut into wedges alongside a dish is mostly not eaten, so this overstates what a serving actually contributes.
keeping: A month in the fridge in a closed bag — four times what they manage in the fruit bowl, where they go hard and dry in a week. Zest before juicing, always, and freeze the zest.

name: lemon juice
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 167747, raw lemon juice. rho 1.03 g/ml.
keeping: Bottled: fridge once opened, 6 months. Freshly squeezed: 3 days in the fridge, or freeze it in an ice cube tray, which is the honest way to use up the half lemon a recipe leaves.

name: lettuce
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169247, romaine. mu 10 g for one leaf.
keeping: A week in the fridge if you wash and spin it dry first, then box it with a sheet of kitchen paper to take up the water it throws off. Wet leaves rot in two days; dry leaves in a sealed box do not.

name: light soy sauce
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 172443, soy sauce from soy and wheat (shoyu). rho 1.08 g/ml, from a tablespoon at 16 g. Chinese light soy sauce (sheng chou) is saltier than Japanese shoyu, so treat the sodium as a floor. Tagged `gluten` for the dietary filters: soy sauce is brewed from soy *and wheat*, and it is the commonest thing to forget on a gluten-free diet. Japanese tamari is the wheat-free one and most Chinese soy sauces are not.
keeping: The cupboard is safe indefinitely, but flavour is a different question: an open bottle oxidises and flattens over about six months. If you get through it slowly, keep it in the fridge, where it holds for a year.

name: lime
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168155, raw. mu 67 g for one lime.
keeping: Three weeks in the fridge in a bag. They dry out faster than lemons and a hard, light lime has no juice in it; roll it hard on the counter before cutting, or microwave it for 10 seconds.

name: lime juice
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168156, raw. rho 1.03 g/ml. One lime gives about 30 ml.
keeping: Fresh lime juice loses its edge within a day of squeezing and is bitter by the third — squeeze it as you need it. Frozen in a tray it holds for 3 months and is better than any bottle.

name: mango
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169910, mangos, raw. mu 200 g is the flesh off one large mango, not the mango — a 350 g fruit gives about that once the stone and skin are gone, and a recipe here weighs the flesh. Alphonso and Ataulfo are the varieties worth buying for a pudding; a stringy fibrous mango purees badly whatever you do to it.
keeping: Ripen it on the counter, never in the fridge, until the shoulders wrinkle slightly and it gives to a thumb at the stem end and smells sweet there. Once ripe, four days in the fridge. Cut flesh keeps two days covered, or freezes in chunks for six months and blends straight from frozen, which is the better answer for a pudding than a sad supermarket mango in February.

name: marsala
sourceNote: Sweet marsala, read across from USDA's sweet dessert wine entry and a bottle label. Most of the energy is the alcohol rather than the sugar. Dry marsala runs about a third fewer calories and would be a different row; the sweet kind is what a dessert uses.

name: mascarpone
sourceNote: From a supermarket tub label, checked in August 2026 against published figures for the cheese, which cluster at 430 to 437 kcal, 5 g protein and 42 to 44 g fat — this row sits inside that spread and its energy reconciles with its own macros, so the macros are left alone; calcium and sodium were the two that were wrong and are corrected here. USDA has no mascarpone record at all, only branded items, which is why this stays a label figure. Mascarpone is barely a cheese — cream soured with acid and drained — which is why it is 44% fat where full-fat cream cheese is nearer 34%, and why a cheesecake made with it needs the acid put back. gramsPerUnit 250 is one standard tub.

name: mint
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 173470, fresh spearmint. rho 0.15 g/ml for loose leaves.
keeping: A week, stems in water on the counter or in the fridge. Never in a sealed bag — mint blackens where it touches plastic.

name: mirin
sourceNote: Hon-mirin, from the Japanese standard composition tables: 241 kcal and 43.2 g of carbohydrate per 100 g at about 14% alcohol. The macros do not add up to the energy and are not meant to — roughly a third of it is the alcohol, which this library has no column for, the same as the wine rows. Most of it boils off in a sauce reduced hard, so treat the figure as an upper bound. Published numbers for mirin range from 150 to 258 kcal because two different products share the name: hon-mirin is brewed and alcoholic, while aji-mirin or 'mirin-style seasoning' is a sweetened syrup at 1% alcohol with corn syrup in it. This row is the real one; the substitute is sweeter and flatter and worth avoiding.
keeping: Three months in a cool cupboard once opened, or a year in the fridge, which is where hon-mirin belongs after opening. The sugar crystallises at the neck and welds the cap on — wipe it. Aji-mirin has preservatives and keeps longer, which is the only argument in its favour.

name: msg
sourceNote: Monosodium glutamate. 12.28 g sodium per 100 g by formula mass (Na 22.99 of C5H8NNaO4 169.11). Contributes no energy at the amounts used. rho 0.8 g/ml as a fine crystal.

name: mussels in the shell
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 174219, raw blue mussel meat, multiplied by a 33% meat yield for the same reason as the clams. Mussels shell out higher than clams and vary with the season; the yield is the assumption in this row.
keeping: The same day. Fridge, in a bowl under a damp cloth, not in water and not in a sealed bag. Debearded mussels die faster than bearded ones, so pull the beards just before cooking.

name: neutral oil
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171030, rapeseed (canola) oil, standing for any neutral cooking oil. Sunflower and groundnut differ in their fatty acids but not in energy. rho 0.92 g/ml.
keeping: A year in a dark cupboard, sealed. Refined oils are the most stable in the kitchen, which is what makes them the right thing to fry in.

name: olive oil
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171413; rho 0.91 g/ml, standard for olive oil at 20 C
keeping: A dark cupboard, away from the hob — heat and light kill it faster than time does. A year sealed, and about three months of good flavour once it is opened.

name: onion
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170000 (raw); mu 110 g, USDA medium onion
keeping: A month somewhere dark and airy, in a paper bag or a basket, never a sealed one and never next to potatoes — each makes the other sprout. A cut half keeps 3 days in the fridge in a box, cut face down; wrapping the cut face is what stops it perfuming the butter.

name: onion powder
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171326. rho 0.5 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 2.4 g.

name: oyster sauce
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 172234. rho 1.2 g/ml, from a tablespoon at 18 g. Tagged `shellfish` and `gluten`: the major brands thicken it with wheat flour as well as cornstarch. Vegetarian 'oyster' sauce made from mushrooms is a straight substitution and carries neither.
keeping: Fridge once opened, and it says so on the bottle. Six months, and use a clean spoon: it is thick enough that anything dropped into it sits there.

name: parmesan
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171247, hard grated parmesan. rho 0.4 g/ml grated. Tagged `meat` as well as `dairy`, which surprises people: Parmigiano Reggiano's DOP rules require calf rennet, so the real thing is not vegetarian. Hard cheeses made with microbial rennet and sold as Italian-style hard cheese are, and are the substitution.
keeping: Six weeks in the fridge wrapped in baking paper and then loosely in foil. Cling film suffocates it and it sweats; paper lets it breathe. Freeze the rinds in a bag and drop one into a soup or a stock.

name: peanut butter
sourceNote: USDA, peanut butter, smooth style, with salt. USDA carries salted and unsalted smooth-style records that differ by little except sodium — 486 mg against about 17 — and this is the salted one, because that is what goes inside a Hong Kong French toast. The id is left off rather than guessed: the two records are easy to confuse and a wrong id is worse than none. rho 1.07 g/ml, from 258 g per cup. A no-added-sugar jar is the same energy with the 9 g of sugar moved into the peanut column.

name: peanut oil
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy, peanut oil (salad or cooking). rho 0.914 g/ml at 20 C. Tagged `peanut` for the dietary filters. Refined groundnut oil is usually tolerated by people with a peanut allergy and is excluded from allergen labelling in the UK for that reason — but cold-pressed and aromatic peanut oils are not, and this row does not know which is in the bottle.
keeping: A year in a dark cupboard. Once it has been used for frying, strain it through a coffee filter while it is still warm and keep it in the fridge; it will take two or three more fryings before it starts to smell fishy, which is when it goes.

name: pecorino romano
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171246, romano cheese. Real Pecorino Romano DOP is saltier than this row says — 1600 mg per 100 g and upwards, since it is brined for months — so treat 1200 as a floor and taste before salting anything it goes into. rho 0.4 g/ml, from a tablespoon of finely grated at 6 g. Tagged `meat` as well as `dairy`: Pecorino Romano DOP is made with lamb rennet and is not vegetarian. An Italian-style hard sheep's cheese with microbial rennet is the substitution, and it is milder.
keeping: A month in the fridge wrapped in baking paper and then loosely in foil, never in cling film, which suffocates it and turns the surface slimy. Buy it in a piece and grate it as you need it: pre-grated pecorino is dry within a week and will not melt into a sauce. Surface mould on a hard cheese is cut off with a centimetre of cheese around it and the rest is fine.

name: pickled chillies
sourceNote: Chinese pickled chillies (泡椒), drained. FoodData Central has no record of them; these are raw chilli figures adjusted for brine, with sodium from a typical jar. The sodium is the figure to distrust — it runs from 1500 to 3000 mg per 100 g by brand.
keeping: Fridge once opened, and they keep six months as long as everything stays under the brine — push them back down with a clean fork each time. Anything sitting proud of the liquid goes soft and then mouldy.

name: pickled mustard greens
sourceNote: Suan cai, the sour pickled mustard green sold in vacuum packs. From packet labels, which mostly print energy and sodium and nothing else; the vitamin C is low because the pickling destroys most of what the fresh green had. The sodium is the figure that matters and it varies enormously — rinsing the leaves takes a third off it and is worth doing.
keeping: A week in the fridge once the pack is open, in a box with any liquid it came with. It is preserved but not sterile, and an opened pack goes slimy at the cut ends first.

name: pork belly
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy, pork fresh belly raw, skin on. Half fat by weight, which is what the cut is — and the figure is for the belly as it goes into the oven. A good deal of that fat renders into the tray during a roast and is poured away, so on a roasted recipe this row overstates what reaches the plate. It is the honest number for the ingredient and the wrong one for the dinner; the recipes that use it say so.

name: pork mince
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168318, lean raw ground pork, interpolated to 5% fat. Fattier mince changes the energy sharply — 20% mince is nearly twice this.
keeping: Two days in the fridge, or freeze flat in a bag for 3 months. Grey on the surface with no smell is oxygen and is fine; grey with a sour smell is not.

name: potato
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170026 (flesh and skin, raw); mu 173 g, USDA medium potato
keeping: A month somewhere dark, cool and airy — a paper bag, never plastic, never the fridge, where the starch turns to sugar and the potato browns unpleasantly when fried. Away from onions. Green skin is solanine and bitter: cut it off, and if it is green throughout, throw it away.

name: prawns
sourceNote: USDA record for crustaceans, shrimp, mixed species, raw — weighed peeled. The sodium is the figure to understand rather than distrust: 566 mg per 100 g looks enormous for a fresh ingredient and is real, because almost all prawns sold peeled have been treated with sodium tripolyphosphate to hold water. Untreated ones run nearer 150 mg. That treatment is also why the protein reads 13.6 g rather than the 20 g an untreated prawn gives: some of what you buy is brine. If the packet says 'prawns' and nothing else, this row is right; if it lists no additives, halve the sodium and expect more protein. mu 12 g is one raw peeled king prawn.
keeping: A day in the fridge, on ice if you have it, in the coldest part — prawns go off faster than almost anything else in this collection and the first sign is a smell of ammonia, at which point they are finished. Most 'fresh' prawns at a counter were frozen at sea and thawed for display, and those must not be refrozen. Frozen raw, three months; defrost in the fridge overnight or in a colander under cold running water for ten minutes, never in warm water. Cook them the day they thaw.

name: preserved bean curd
sourceNote: Fu yu, the fermented tofu sold in jars of brine — USDA SR Legacy 174280, salted and fermented tofu. gramsPerUnit 12 is one cube. Its brine is the same product with more water in it, so a recipe that uses a spoonful of the liquid can count it as more of the cube without introducing a real error. The red kind (nan ru, cured with red yeast rice) is sweeter and deeper and would want its own row if a recipe called for it.
keeping: A year in the fridge once opened, as long as the cubes stay under the brine. Top the jar up with a splash of shaoxing wine rather than water if the level drops.

name: preserved egg
sourceNote: Pidan, the century egg. USDA has no record for it. Protein 13.1 g, fat 10.7 g and carbohydrate 2.25 g per 100 g come from the peer-reviewed comparison of pidan against fresh and salted duck egg (PubMed 26760738); the energy figure is those three put through the Atwater factors rather than measured. Sodium, cholesterol and iron are converted from a shelled preserved duck egg product panel quoting a 60 g egg, which is also where mu 60 g comes from. Saturated fat is derived: raw duck egg is 26.7% of its fat saturated, applied to pidan's 10.7 g. Everything else is deliberately blank — curing in alkali and salt for weeks changes an egg's minerals in ways nobody has published a full table for, and a blank column is honest where a copied duck-egg figure would not be.
keeping: Three months in the cupboard unopened, in the clay or the vacuum pack they came in — they are already preserved, which is the whole point of them, and the fridge does nothing for them. Once peeled, two days in the fridge in a covered bowl. A good one has a translucent amber-brown white that yields like firm jelly and a dark green-grey yolk still soft at the centre; throw away any whose white has gone opaque and crumbly, or that smells strongly of ammonia rather than faintly of it.

name: puff pastry
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 172790, puff pastry, frozen, ready-to-bake — raw, as bought. mu 320 g is one standard rolled sheet. The saturated fat is the figure to hold loosely: this record is a vegetable-shortening pastry, high in polyunsaturated fat, and an all-butter puff of the same energy carries roughly twice the saturated fat. All-butter is what an egg tart wants, so read that column as a floor.
keeping: Two days in the fridge in its own paper, and it must stay cold — pastry that has warmed enough to feel greasy has had its butter layers merge and will not rise. A month in the freezer, and it defrosts in the fridge overnight, never on the counter. Do not refreeze a sheet you have thawed; roll the offcuts into a block rather than a ball, so the layers stay stacked, and it will still puff on a second use.

name: rice vinegar
sourceNote: Unseasoned Japanese-style rice vinegar, from bottle labels: 18 kcal per 100 ml, essentially all of it from residual carbohydrate. Seasoned rice vinegar (sushi-su) is a different thing entirely — around 15 g of sugar and over 1000 mg of sodium per 100 ml — and would need its own row.

name: sake
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 167723, alcoholic beverage, rice (sake). As with the wine rows, most of the energy is alcohol rather than the 5 g of carbohydrate, so the macros will not sum to it and most of it boils off anyway. Cooking sake sold as ryorishu is salted, which this row is not; if that is what is in the cupboard, count roughly 200 mg of sodium per 100 ml and take it off the salt elsewhere. Dry sherry is the usual substitute and is close enough.
keeping: Unopened, a year somewhere cool and dark. Once open it oxidises like wine: a month in the fridge for cooking, though a drinking sake is past its best within days. It does not go dangerous, it goes flat and faintly sherried, which for a braise matters much less than for a glass.

name: salt
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 173468 (table salt); rho 273 g per cup; sodium by stoichiometry

name: salted duck egg
sourceNote: Whole salted duck egg, shell off — white and yolk together. Energy, protein, fat and cholesterol from the Chinese food composition table's entry for xian ya dan; the cholesterol is high because a duck yolk is large and this is most of one. gramsPerUnit 60 is the edible part of one egg, of which roughly 18 g is yolk. The sodium is the weak figure and deliberately a middle one: sources run from 1300 to 2700 mg per 100 g depending on how long the egg was cured, so a recipe using these will be within a factor of two rather than exact. A recipe that uses only the yolks is saltier per gram than this row and less so per egg, since most of the salt is in the white.
keeping: Two months uncooked in the fridge, still in their coating if they came in one. They are cured, so they are far more forgiving than a fresh egg — but once cooked they keep only 4 days.

name: salted fish
sourceNote: Chinese salted fish — mackerel or threadfin, salted and dried. Figures from the Chinese food composition table's entry for xian yu; no USDA equivalent exists. The sodium is the load-bearing number and the least certain: curing time and whether the fish was rinsed both move it, and 6000 mg per 100 g is a middle value across a wide spread.

name: savoiardi
sourceNote: Italian ladyfingers, from packet labels. gramsPerUnit 8.5 is one biscuit, so a 200 g box is about 24. The cholesterol is high for a biscuit because savoiardi are largely egg — which is also why they are dry and crisp enough to take up coffee without collapsing, where a soft sponge finger cannot.

name: sesame oil
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171029. rho 0.92 g/ml. Toasted sesame oil is used as a seasoning here rather than a frying medium, except in the three-cup chicken where it is both.
keeping: Six months in a dark cupboard once opened, a year in the fridge. Toasted sesame oil goes rancid faster than most oils, and since it is used a teaspoon at a time the bottle usually outlives its flavour.

name: sesame paste
sourceNote: USDA record for sesame butter or paste, made from whole seeds — which is what Chinese sesame paste is. It is not tahini: tahini is ground from hulled and usually unroasted seeds and is paler, thinner and much milder, and swapping it into a tantanmen gives a broth that tastes of nothing. The two are close enough in composition that these figures stand for either. Calcium is 960 mg per 100 g, which is real and comes from the hulls. rho 1.05 g/ml.
keeping: A year unopened in the cupboard, six months in the fridge once open. It separates into a hard cake under a layer of oil and that is normal — stand the jar in warm water and stir it back with a knife, and store it upside down between uses so the oil migrates the other way. Rancid sesame paste smells sharp and paint-like and there is no rescuing it.

name: shallot
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170439, raw. mu 40 g for one banana shallot, peeled; USDA's own 10 g figure is for a single small round shallot, which is not what a recipe calling for 'a shallot' means.
keeping: The same as onions, dark and airy, a month. They dry out faster than onions do, so a shallot that has gone papery and light has nothing left in it.

name: shaoxing wine
sourceNote: Shaoxing rice wine, from a typical bottle rather than FoodData Central. Cooking grades are salted, which is where the sodium comes from; drinking grades are not. Most of the alcohol boils off in step 9, so treat the energy as an upper bound. Tagged `alcohol` and `gluten`: shaoxing is fermented with a wheat starter as well as rice. Dry sherry is the usual substitute and is wheat-free; for a no-alcohol version, use stock with a splash of rice vinegar and accept that it is a different dish.
keeping: The cupboard, a year, cap on. It is a fortified cooking wine and does not turn the way a table wine does — it just gets duller, and a bottle that has been open two years is worth replacing.

name: sichuan chilli powder
sourceNote: Ground dried chilli — erjingtiao or facing-heaven, the coarse red powder Sichuan cooking uses by the spoon. Nutritionally it is the same thing as USDA SR Legacy 171329 (ground red pepper), which is what these figures are, and it is a separate row only because it is a separate ingredient in a recipe: `chilli powder` in this library is the American blend with cumin and salt in it, and using that here would be wrong twice over. rho 0.5 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 2.5 g — powder packs denser than the flakes row.
keeping: Six months in a sealed jar out of the light, or a year in the freezer, which is worth it for a bag bought in any real quantity. Colour is the tell: bright red is alive, brown is over.

name: sichuan peppercorn oil
sourceNote: Hua jiao you: a neutral or rapeseed oil infused with Sichuan peppercorn, so it is nutritionally the oil it was made from and is entered as such. rho 0.92 g/ml, as for other seed oils. It goes in by the teaspoon at the end and never as a frying medium — heating it drives off the numbing aromatic that is the whole point of it.
keeping: Six months in a dark cupboard. Its whole point is a volatile aroma, so it fades rather than spoils; a bottle that no longer prickles when you smell it is finished, whatever the date says.

name: silken tofu
sourceNote: USDA soft silken tofu. A third of the protein and a twentieth of the calcium of the `firm tofu` row, because silken tofu is barely pressed and is set with GDL or nigari rather than calcium sulfate — the two are not interchangeable in a recipe or in this table. gramsPerUnit 300 is a standard tube or box.
keeping: Use it the day you open it. Submerged in water in the fridge it holds for 2 days, and it will have wept and softened by then. Never freeze it.

name: smoked paprika
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170934, paprika. Smoking changes the flavour and not the composition. rho 0.46 g/ml.

name: soba
sourceNote: Dried buckwheat noodles, weighed dry. Published figures cluster at 336 to 353 kcal and this takes the bottom of that, which reconciles with its own macros. The real variable is not the brand's arithmetic but its buckwheat content: cheap soba can be 30% buckwheat and 70% wheat, juwari soba is 100% buckwheat and costs four times as much, and the protein and mineral columns move with that. Check the packet if it matters to you. Sodium is low here because it is a Japanese dried noodle salted in the dough; some brands run several times this. mu 100 g is one portion. Tagged `gluten`: most soba is 30 to 70% wheat. Juwari soba is 100% buckwheat and is the exception, and it says so on the packet.
keeping: A year in the packet in a dry cupboard. Cooked soba is the least forgiving noodle in this collection: rinsed and iced it is good for an hour, and after that it stiffens and goes chalky whatever you do. Cook it to order.

name: sour cream
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171256, cultured sour cream, full fat. rho 0.96 g/ml. Crème fraîche is the richer substitute at about 40% fat against this 19%, and swapping one for the other changes a filling's energy by more than the difference looks.

name: spaghetti
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168927, dry unenriched pasta. Enriched pasta carries considerably more iron and folate; check the packet if either matters.

name: spinach
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168462, spinach, raw, weighed raw — which is what a recipe lists, though it collapses to about a seventh of its volume and a fifth of its weight once blanched and squeezed. Sold by weight, so no per-item figure. The iron figure is real and the reputation is overstated: spinach is high in oxalate, which binds a good deal of that iron before anyone absorbs it.
keeping: Four days in the fridge in its bag with a sheet of kitchen paper in it to take up the condensation, which is what actually turns a bag of spinach to slime. Wash it only when you use it. Blanched and squeezed into balls it keeps three days or freezes for three months, and frozen spinach is genuinely fine for anything where it will be squeezed dry anyway — which includes every recipe here that uses it.

name: spring onions
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170005, raw scallions. mu 15 g for one; rho 0.25 g/ml chopped.
keeping: Two weeks in the fridge wrapped in a damp cloth inside a bag. Or stand them root-down in 2 cm of water on the windowsill, change the water every other day, and they keep growing — a bunch gives two or three cuttings before it gives up.

name: suan cai yu kit
sourceNote: A packet of Sichuan pickled cabbage fish seasoning. Baijia (bai jia) sells a 300 g one in British Chinese supermarkets for a little over two pounds, and Haorenjia, Qiaotou and Tianwei make the same thing. Inside are three sachets: the pickled mustard greens, which are the bulk of the weight, a small seasoning oil, and a smaller powder for marinating the fish. **No manufacturer publishes a nutrition panel for these in a form that could be verified here**, so this row is built rather than read. Taking the greens at this library's own pickled mustard greens row (25 kcal, 2000 mg of sodium) and the oil-and-powder sachets at roughly 300 kcal and 3800 mg, a packet that is 70% greens by weight comes to about 108 kcal and 2540 mg per 100 g, which is what is recorded. The greens share is the uncertain part and runs from about 60% to 90% between brands — most packets print the sachet weights on the front, so a specific one can be worked out exactly. Read any panel using this as indicative. What is not in doubt is that the sodium is high: a packet seasons a kilo of food and is mostly salt and pickle. mu 300 g is one packet. Tagged `soy` for the dietary filters, from the seasoning sachets rather than the greens; as with everything else about this packet, the printed panel is the authority.
keeping: A year in the sealed packet in a cupboard. Once open the sachets should be used at once: the greens ferment on in the fridge and go soft and unpleasantly sour within a week, and the oil sachet has nothing to keep it in. If you only want half a packet, freeze the rest of the greens in their liquid, which works, and accept that the oil sachet does not divide neatly.

name: sweet potato
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168482, sweet potato, raw, unprepared. mu 130 g is one medium tuber peeled. The vitamin A figure is the orange-fleshed sort and is enormous — one portion of the ginger syrup is several days' worth. A white or purple-fleshed sweet potato has almost none of it and is otherwise the same food.
keeping: Two weeks in a cool dark place in paper, and never the fridge, which turns the starch hard and gives a gritty core no amount of cooking softens. Cut surfaces brown within minutes: drop peeled chunks into cold water if you are not cooking them straight away. A soft or shrivelled patch means it has started to go and cuts out; a smell of paint stripper means the whole tuber is finished.

name: sweetcorn
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 168536, canned sweetcorn with liquid. Draining it takes out most of the sodium; creamed corn is thicker and slightly sweeter.
keeping: Cook it the day you buy it if it is on the cob: the sugar starts turning to starch the moment it is picked, and a two-day-old cob is measurably duller. Kernels off the cob freeze perfectly.

name: tapioca pearls
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169717, tapioca, pearl, dry — weighed dry, which is how a recipe lists it, and they roughly quadruple in weight once boiled. Sold as sago in most British supermarkets: true sago comes from a palm and tapioca from cassava, and what is in the packet is almost always tapioca whatever the label says. Nutritionally it is starch and nothing else. Watch the unit when reading this record elsewhere — several sites quote 544 kcal, which is a 152 g cup rather than 100 g.

name: taro
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169227, taro, raw — the corm, not the leaves, which USDA carries separately and which are a different vegetable. Carbohydrate is 26.46 g and not the 23.4 some sites report: that lower figure is carbohydrate with the 4.1 g of fibre already taken out, and 26.46 is the one that reconciles with the 112 kcal. Sold by weight and in wildly different sizes, from a 200 g cocoyam to a 2 kg dasheen, so there is no per-item figure.
keeping: Two weeks somewhere cool, dark and dry, in paper and never plastic, and never the fridge — cold turns the corm hard and grey. Buy one that is firm all over with no soft or mouldy patches at the cut end, and check it is not woody by pressing: it should feel like a raw potato. Once peeled it browns and dries within an hour, so cook it the same day. Peeled cubes freeze for three months and go straight into a pan from frozen, which is easier than fresh and barely worse.

name: thai basil
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 172232, fresh basil. Thai basil is a different cultivar with the same composition to within the precision of this table. rho 0.1 g/ml for loose leaves.
keeping: On the counter, stems in water, out of the fridge entirely: below about 7 degrees the leaves blacken overnight. Three days is what you get, so buy it for the day.

name: toasted sesame seeds
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170151, whole sesame seeds roasted and toasted. rho 0.6 g/ml, from a tablespoon at 9 g. The calcium is in the hull, so hulled (decorticated) seeds carry roughly a tenth of it — this row is for the unhulled kind sold for sprinkling.
keeping: Six months in a sealed jar in the cupboard, a year in the freezer. They are half fat and they are already toasted, so rancidity is what ends them: a sharp, crayon-like smell means throw them out.

name: tomato
