sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170457 (red, ripe, raw); mu 123 g, USDA medium tomato
keeping: On the counter, stem-side down, out of the sun. Never the fridge below full ripeness: under about 12 degrees the flesh goes mealy and the smell never comes back. Once dead ripe, the fridge buys 3 days.

name: tomato paste
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170054, canned tomato paste with no salt added. rho 1.1 g/ml, from a tablespoon at 16 g. A salted paste runs several hundred milligrams of sodium per 100 g above this; check the tin.

name: turkey breast
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 171506, raw skinless turkey breast.
keeping: Two days in the fridge. Cooked turkey keeps 3 days and is drier every one of them; slice what is left, cover it with its own juices or a little stock, and it stays edible to the third.

name: udon noodles
sourceNote: Boiled udon — the pre-cooked vacuum-packed or frozen kind a recipe drops straight into a bowl, which is what the weight in a recipe here refers to. Japanese standard composition tables give 95 to 105 kcal for it and English-language sources run to 124; this row takes 105, which reconciles with its own macros. **Dried udon is a different row's worth of numbers** — about three times the energy per gram before it is cooked — so weigh what goes in the bowl, not what comes out of the packet. The sodium is real and is in the noodle rather than the soup: udon dough is salted, which is what gives it the bite. mu 150 g is the single-serving pack. mu 200 g is one vacuum-packed or frozen sanuki portion, which is the pack size every British Asian supermarket sells — Yutaka, TS Tanoshiya and the frozen brands are all 200 g. It was recorded as 150 g here until the count started being shown on the recipe line, where it read as two and a half portions for a two-portion dish and gave itself away.
keeping: Vacuum-packed, up to the date on the pack in the fridge, and they are best frozen — frozen udon is the better product anyway, thicker and chewier than chilled, and goes into boiling water straight from the freezer. Once the pack is open they dry at the surface within a day, so cook the lot. Cooked and left in soup they turn to paste within an hour, which is why the soup and the noodles are kept apart in this collection.

name: unsalted butter
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 173430; rho from the 227 g (2-stick) US cup
keeping: A month in the fridge, wrapped, and 6 months in the freezer. Butter takes up smells through its wrapper, so it does not go next to the garlic or the fish; a stale, cheesy smell at the surface is rancidity and does not cook out.

name: vanilla extract
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 173470. Most of the 288 kcal is the alcohol it is extracted into. rho 0.88 g/ml, from a teaspoon at 4.2 g — and at a teaspoon a time it cannot move a panel, which is the case for entering it at all rather than leaving it as a coverage gap. Tagged `alcohol`: real extract is vanilla macerated in roughly 35% alcohol, and while a baked cake drives most of it off, a no-alcohol filter is usually asked about the ingredient rather than the chemistry. Alcohol-free vanilla flavouring exists.

name: wakame
sourceNote: Dried wakame flakes, which is what is sold and what a recipe weighs — 5 g of it becomes a bowlful. USDA carries only raw wakame (45 kcal, 3.03 g protein, 872 mg sodium per 100 g), so these figures are that record scaled for moisture: raw wakame is about 80% water and the dried flakes about 9%, a factor of 4.55, and the scaled numbers sit inside the range printed on dried packets. Published dried figures scatter widely, sodium most of all, because how much of the salting brine is left in it differs by producer. It rehydrates about ten times over, so weigh it dry and be conservative.
keeping: A year in a sealed bag in a dark cupboard; there is nothing in it to spoil and what it loses is colour and aroma. It is hygroscopic, so a bag left open goes limp and clumps, and once it has taken up damp it will not crisp again. Rehydrated wakame keeps two days in the fridge and no longer.

name: walnuts
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170187, English walnuts. rho 0.5 g/ml for roughly chopped halves, 120 g per cup.
keeping: The freezer, in a bag, a year — this is one of the few things genuinely worth freezing by default. Walnuts have the most fragile fat of any common nut and go bitter in a cupboard within about two months of opening.

name: water
sourceNote: Tap water. No energy and no macronutrients; the trace minerals vary entirely with where you live and are given only so that a recipe listing water resolves rather than reporting a gap.

name: white bread
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 172686, bread, white, commercially prepared. mu 30 g is one ordinary supermarket slice; the thick-cut sort a Hong Kong French toast wants is nearer 40 g, so a recipe calling for thick slices by weight rather than by count is telling the truth and one calling for four slices is estimating. UK sliced white runs lower in sodium than this American record — about 360 mg per 100 g against 477 — because the salt reduction targets here are stricter.
keeping: Three days in the bread bin at room temperature, in paper or its own bag but never the fridge, which stales bread faster than the counter does — the starch retrogrades quickest just above zero. Three months sliced and frozen, and it toasts straight from frozen. Stale bread is not waste: it is what French toast, breadcrumbs and a bread pudding are actually for, and it soaks custard better than fresh.

name: white cabbage
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 169975, raw green cabbage — the dense pale drumhead sold as white cabbage here. gramsPerUnit 900 is a small whole head. A different row from `chinese cabbage`, which is a fifth of the fibre and cooks in a quarter of the time.

name: white fish fillets
sourceNote: A deliberately generic row for the mild, firm, boneless white fish these recipes slice thin — basa or pangasius, which is what a Chinese supermarket freezer has and what a suan cai yu is made with here, and which these figures are for. Tilapia is within a few per cent of it. Sea bass and cod are leaner and rather more expensive and would each read a little lower in fat. Grass carp, the traditional fish, is not sold in Britain in any form. The row is generic because the dish is: what matters is that the fillet is thick enough to slice on the diagonal and firm enough to hold together in a boiling broth. mu 150 g is one fillet.
keeping: One day in the fridge on the bottom shelf if fresh, and most white fish sold as fresh was frozen at sea and thawed for display, in which case it must not be refrozen and should be cooked the day it is bought. Frozen fillets keep six months and are genuinely better than tired fresh ones for this — defrost overnight in the fridge, then press between kitchen paper, because a wet fillet will not take a cornflour coating. Fish that smells of anything beyond the sea is finished.

name: white pepper
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 170932, ground white pepper. rho 0.47 g/ml, from a level teaspoon at 2.3 g.

name: white vinegar
sourceNote: USDA SR Legacy 173469, distilled vinegar, 5% acidity. Nutritionally it is water: it earns its place in a recipe for the acid, not for anything in this row.

name: wonton wrappers
sourceNote: USDA record for wonton wrappers, including egg roll wrappers — the square yellow sheets sold fresh or frozen in every Asian supermarket. mu 6 g is one 8 cm square; a standard pack of 250 g is about forty. The sodium is in the dough and is why a wonton needs less salt in its filling than it looks like it should. Thicker dumpling and gyoza wrappers are the same composition in a heavier sheet.
keeping: A week in the fridge in the packet, sealed — the top sheet dries out and cracks within an hour of being opened, so keep the stack under a damp cloth while you work and re-wrap what is left. Three months in the freezer, and thaw them in the fridge rather than on the counter, which sweats them into a solid block. Wrapped wontons freeze better than wrappers do: freeze them apart on a tray, then bag them, and boil from frozen.

name: ya cai
sourceNote: Yibin sui mi ya cai (宜宾碎米芽菜) — mustard stems and leaves chopped to rice-grain size, salted, sun-dried and then fermented, which is why the carbohydrate figure looks so high for a pickle: it is a dried product, not a wet one. FoodData Central has no record. Energy and macros are the Chinese composition table's figures for ya cai, which reconcile with each other (4.9x4 + 35.7x4 + 1.3x9 = 174). Sodium is the uncertain one and is recorded at the middle of the 1000 to 2000 mg range the published analyses give; how much of the salting brine is left in it differs by producer, and the packet is the authority. The iron figure of 27.7 mg is what the tables say and is startling; a 40 g portion is not the iron supplement that arithmetic suggests, because absorption from a fermented plant is another question entirely. A different row from `zha cai`, which is the knobbly stem pickle, and from `pickled mustard greens`, which are the wet sour ones sold in brine — ya cai is dry, sweet-salty and dark brown, and substituting either of the others gives a different dish. mu 100 g is one packet.
keeping: Two months in the fridge in a sealed box once the packet is open, and it barely changes in that time — it is dry and very salty and there is little in it left to spoil. Unopened it keeps a year in the cupboard. It does not need rinsing and should not be rinsed: the salt and the sweetness are the seasoning the dish is built on, which is why recipes using it add less soy sauce than they look like they should.

name: zha cai
sourceNote: Preserved mustard stem, the knobbly Sichuan pickle sold shredded in foil packets. Sodium from the Chinese food composition table's entry for zha cai, around 4250 mg per 100 g — it is the saltiest thing in most kitchens, and 40 g of it carries more salt than a quarter teaspoon of salt does. Sold as Yuquan (yu quan) preserved mustard stem in 80 g foil packets in any British Chinese supermarket, for well under a pound, in plain and hot chilli versions — the chilli one is the commoner and is what these recipes assume. mu 80 g is one packet, which is about the amount two dishes here use.
keeping: A month in the fridge in a sealed box once opened. Very salty and very dry, so it keeps far better than the pickled greens do — but it takes up smells, so it needs a lid rather than a plate over it.
